title: Size, morphology and ecology explain interspecific differences in the use of bird bills and legs as thermal windows
content:
Read the free Plain Language Summary for this article on the Journal blog.


Abstract

Birds use their bills and legs as thermal windows, increasing near-surface blood flow to dissipate heat in hot conditions while restricting blood flow to conserve heat in cold conditions. How adept species are at vasomotor control of heat loss via bills and legs may influence their capacity to adapt to a warming climate. However, whether and how species vary in their capacity to control heat loss via thermal windows is poorly understood. We used infrared thermography of wild birds in their natural habitat to estimate vasomotor control of heat loss via bird bills and legs across a diverse range of species (N = 12 species). We investigated ecological drivers of interspecific variation in estimated vasomotor control of heat loss via bird bills and legs in response to microclimate conditions. We further used morphological measurements of museum specimens to test whether variation in estimated vasomotor control of heat loss relates to morphological responses to climatic warming. Species differ significantly in how much they adjust their bill surface temperature with changing air temperature. By contrast, we found minimal interspecific variation in estimated vasomotor control of heat loss via legs. Water-associated species have superior vasomotor control of heat loss via their appendages compared to terrestrial foraging species. Larger species and species with longer bills have greater vasomotor control of heat loss via their bills. Interspecific variation (or lack thereof) in vasomotor control of heat loss via appendages may have important implications for birds under a warming climate. However, we found no convincing evidence that interspecific variation in estimated vasomotor control of heat loss via bills corresponds with changes in bill size over time.
